primary_text_note: In copyright (Hill, 1983). Quotations verified against LitCharts, Shmoop, RevisionWorld and a quotation compilation; SparkNotes/GradeSaver were unreachable.

findings.claim: Repeated claim that the section is a two-part question: 'part (a) asks you to analyse the extract (20 marks - AO1, AO2), and part (b) asks about the wider text (20 marks - AO1, AO2, AO4)'; L8 'Post-1914 prose questions ... typically pair a printed extract with a wider-text task'; L8 knowledge check 'What are the two parts of the ... question?'; every practice question labelled '20 marks'.
findings.truth: Section A is ONE source-based question worth 40 marks, with an extract from the set text printed on the paper. There is no part (a) / part (b) and no 20+20 split. Component 2 lasts 2 hours 30 minutes and is closed book.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md section 2.2: Component 2, 2h30, Section A Post 1914 Prose/Drama, 40 marks, source based response, 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4', closed book; section 3.1 defines AO3 as context and AO4 as vocabulary/sentence structures/accuracy

findings.field: content_html / exam_tip_html / conclusion_html / glossary_terms / flashcard_questions / knowledge_checks
findings.claim: AO4 is defined throughout as context: 'Assessment Objective 4: Show understanding of the relationship between texts and the contexts in which they were written', 'AO4 specifically rewards understanding of context', 'For Eduqas AO4 ... show how context shapes Hill's writing choices', 'AO4 = context (part b only)', and a knowledge check whose key says AO4 is the objective tested in part (b) but not part (a).
findings.truth: That is the spec wording for AO3. AO4 is 'Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation'. Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only, so context is NOT a credited objective on this question; AO4 marks are for the accuracy of the student's own writing. Telling students that context earns marks here is mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md section 2.2: Component 2, 2h30, Section A Post 1914 Prose/Drama, 40 marks, source based response, 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4', closed book; section 3.1 defines AO3 as context and AO4 as vocabulary/sentence structures/accuracy

findings.claim: The board is named in student-facing text: 'essential for the Eduqas exam', heading 'The Eduqas Context: Why This Matters', 'For Eduqas AO4', 'For Eduqas, remember the assessment objectives', 'Which AO assesses context in Eduqas literature?', and the L8 description 'plus Eduqas exam technique for Component 2 Section A'.
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board. Reworded to neutral phrasing ('your prose question', 'this question', 'the post-1914 prose question'). The L8 description was also 134 characters, over the 100-character limit; the rewrite is 96.
findings.evidence: house rule feedback_eduqas_wjec_neutral_phrasing

findings.claim: Quoted as Hill's wording: skin 'tautly stretched and thin, so that the bones of her face showed through' and 'bones showing through'.
findings.truth: The novel (ch. 4) reads: 'only the thinnest layer of flesh was tautly stretched and strained across her bones'. 'Thin, so that the bones of her face showed through' is not Hill's wording.
findings.evidence: Shmoop appearance quotes, ch. 4: https://www.shmoop.com/study-guides/woman-in-black/appearances-quotes.html

findings.claim: 'It is during the funeral that Arthur notices a figure ... : "a woman, dressed in deepest black, her face partly hidden by a veil."' plus the same 'tautly stretched and thin ... bones of her face showed through' misquotation.
findings.truth: The novel reads 'She was dressed in deepest black, in the style of full mourning that had rather gone out of fashion'. She wears a bonnet, not a veil. Both quotations were rewritten to the real wording.
findings.evidence: Shmoop appearance quotes, ch. 4; LitCharts ch. 4

findings.claim: Two flashcards attribute the Eel Marsh House warning to Keckwick: 'Which Keckwick line warns Arthur off Eel Marsh House?' and 'Which warning does Keckwick offer Arthur about Eel Marsh House?'
findings.truth: The lesson's own content gives the line to Samuel Daily, and Daily is the character who warns Arthur. Keckwick is the pony-and-trap driver and barely speaks.
findings.evidence: LitCharts plot summary: 'Samuel warns Arthur that he would be a fool to return to Eel Marsh House'

findings.claim: Malformed student-facing text: 'What whose funeral brings Arthur to Crythin Gifford?' and 'The belief reason and logic ... guide understanding' (twice).
findings.truth: Missing words. Corrected.
findings.evidence: n/a

findings.claim: 'Hill describes it as "grey, tall, gaunt, like some bony old woman"' is taught as THE key quotation for Eel Marsh House across two lessons: in content, in the takeaways, in a gap-fill knowledge check, on four flashcards and in two practice questions.
findings.truth: That simile is not in the novel. Chapter 5 reads 'a tall, gaunt house of grey stone with a slate roof', and the simile in that passage is 'It stood like some lighthouse or beacon or martello tower'. The analysis was re-anchored on the real wording: 'gaunt' is a word for a starved human body, which still carries the link to Jennet's 'wasted face'.
findings.evidence: Chapter 5 text quoted at https://gcseenglishteacher.com/2014/10/21/woman-in-black-chapter-5-analysis/ and the margot_quotes compilation

findings.claim: 'Arthur is working in the house when he hears, from the direction of the marshes, the unmistakable sounds of a horse and cart ... Arthur rushes outside and finds "nothing. No pony, no trap, no child. Nothing."'
findings.truth: In chapter 6 Arthur is OUT on the marsh when the sea fret closes in; the sounds come out of the mist around him and he cannot see because of the fret. He does not hear them indoors and run out.
findings.evidence: LitCharts plot summary, ch. 6: 'he hears the sound of a pony trap approaching, but the noise seems to be everywhere and nowhere at once - a thick mist has rolled in'

findings.claim: Three lessons state that Arthur forces the nursery door: 'eventually forces it open', 'until Arthur forces the door', 'Arthur forces the nursery door open', 'He forces open the locked nursery'.
findings.truth: Arthur cannot open the locked door. He goes to fetch an axe to break it down and returns to find the door already ajar - the room opens itself. The distinction matters because the transgression reading in L7 is built on it.
findings.evidence: LitCharts plot summary: 'he returns inside to knock down the door, but finds that it is ajar'

findings.claim: 'She died of a "wasting disease"' - given as Jennet's cause of death in three lessons (including a glossary tooltip) and on a flashcard.
findings.truth: The death certificates in the packet of letters record that Jennet died twelve years after Nathaniel, aged 36, of heart failure. 'Wasting disease' is Arthur's guess at the funeral about the appearance of the figure he sees; it is not the recorded cause of death.
findings.evidence: LitCharts ch. 11 summary (three death certificates; 'Jennet died twelve years later at age 36 from heart failure')

findings.claim: 'Sam Daily explains: "Whenever she has been seen... in some way, a child has died."'
findings.truth: The novel reads: 'And whenever she has been seen ... however briefly, and whoever by, there has been one sure and certain result.' The lesson set a paraphrase in quotation marks.
findings.evidence: margot_quotes compilation of the novel's text

findings.claim: 'Her expression combines "desperate, wild, grief" with "malevolence"' - repeated in the exam tip's model sentence and used as the stem of a gap-fill knowledge check.
findings.truth: The novel's phrase is a single one: 'a desperate, yearning malevolence'. 'Desperate, wild, grief' does not appear. The gap-fill answer (malevolence) stays correct once the stem is corrected.
findings.evidence: LitCharts ch. 5 quotes: 'a desperate, yearning malevolence; it was as though she were searching for something she wanted, needed - must have'

findings.claim: 'Sam's wife has also been affected by the curse - she has "premonitions" and "bad feelings" about Eel Marsh House' and 'Sam Daily's wife has "premonitions" that damage her mental health.'
findings.truth: No source supports this. What the novel gives is that Samuel Daily and his wife take Arthur into their home and nurse him after his collapse. The invented detail was replaced with supported material.
findings.evidence: LitCharts character notes: 'He and his wife tend to Arthur as he recovers from his fright'

findings.claim: The novel's closing lines quoted as 'They asked me for my story. I have told it. Enough.'
findings.truth: The text reads 'They asked for my story. I have told it. Enough.' - no 'me'. This is a line students memorise.
findings.evidence: LitCharts ch. 12 quote: 'I had seen the ghost of Jennet Humfrye and she had had her revenge. They asked for my story. I have told it. Enough.'

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Who is Mr Jerome in The Woman in Black?' answer 'The estate's solicitor'.
findings.truth: Jerome is the local land agent. Arthur Kipps is the solicitor, sent by Mr Bentley's London firm. The same lesson's body text correctly calls Jerome 'Mrs Drablow's local agent', so the card contradicts the lesson.
findings.evidence: LitCharts character list: 'Mr. Jerome: a real estate agent in Crythin Gifford'

findings.claim: 'The small graveyard near Eel Marsh House contains the graves of the Drablow family and, eventually, Jennet and Nathaniel ... Arthur discovers that Nathaniel's grave is separate from the family plot, reflecting his status as an illegitimate child excluded from the family even in death.'
findings.truth: This scene does not happen. Chapter 5 gives the ruins of a small chapel and a burial ground of about fifty neglected gravestones; no names are read out and there is no family plot or separate grave. It is in that burial ground that Arthur sees the woman in black for the second time. The paragraph was rewritten to the verified detail while keeping the social-exclusion theme.
findings.evidence: LitCharts ch. 5 summary (ruined chapel, ~50 gravestones, 'a decayed, abandoned air'); ch. 11 summary says nothing about burial

findings.claim: Practice question text: 'Write a Band 5 paragraph analysing Hill's use of language ...'
findings.truth: There is no 'Band 5' on this qualification and it does not match the house band ladder. Changed to 'a top-band paragraph'.
findings.evidence: house band ladder

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions are labelled '20 marks - Extract Analysis' or '20 marks - Wider Text Response', and all 48 mark schemes use a 20-mark band ladder (Top band 17-20 down to Lower band 1-4).
findings.truth: The real question is worth 40 marks. Every label was changed to '40 marks - Source-based response' (extract focus / whole-text focus), and every band ladder rescaled to 33-40 / 25-32 / 17-24 / 9-16 / 1-8. Several mark schemes also carried the corrected quotations and the AO4-as-context error; those strings were corrected in the same edit.

findings.claim: A cluster of quotations that no online source reproduces, so they could not be checked against the novel: 'a young man, healthy, optimistic, with a future before me' (L1, L2, L5); the marshes as 'wide and grey and empty, stretching away on all sides' (L3, L7) AND as 'the marshes stretched in every direction... desolate, grey, empty' (L1, L6, L8) - two different 'quotations' for the same description; 'peculiar, intense silence, broken only by the lapping of the water' (L3, L6); fog 'thick, damp, clinging' (L6, L7, L8); 'I did not then know what I know now' (L6); 'You don't want to go there... It isn't a place I'd choose to spend an hour' (L2, L5); 'The pony swerved and bolted, the trap overturned... Stella and our son were thrown' (L4); 'desperate, afraid, in a state of near panic' (L3, L5); 'she could not bear to be parted from him' (L5); Spider 'yelping, howling' (L3); the nursery contents 'a small bed, a chest of toys, a child's chair, clothes' (L3).
findings.truth: The text is in copyright and none of these appear in any fetchable source, so I could not prove them wrong and did not edit them. Two things make me uneasy: the same marsh description is quoted with two different wordings in different lessons, and the verified quotations in this unit were wrong more often than right. Options: (a) leave them, (b) check them against a copy of the novel in one pass and re-edit, (c) demote them to paraphrase (drop the quotation marks). Recommendation: (b) - a single pass with the book open, since the marsh quotation carries a whole tricolon analysis and a practice question.
findings.evidence: no fetchable source; SparkNotes/GradeSaver blocked or timed out

findings.claim: The Spider collapsible in L3 (headed 'Chapters 5-8') narrates the marsh rescue: 'Spider runs towards the marshes and becomes trapped ... Arthur has to wade into the freezing water to rescue her.'
findings.truth: That rescue is chapter 10 ('Whistle and I'll Come to You'), outside the lesson's stated span. Spider is only lent to Arthur in chapter 8. Not wrong as a fact, only out of the lesson's range, and L4 does not repeat it.
findings.evidence: chapter list in the brief

findings.claim: L4 says 'Hill uses an epistolary technique to reveal Jennet's backstory.'
findings.truth: The novel embeds a packet of letters and death certificates but is not an epistolary novel. The glossary definition given is loose enough to be defensible, so no edit.
findings.evidence: n/a

summary: No lesson was clean. The unit taught the wrong exam format throughout - an invented two-part 20+20 question with AO4 defined as context - when the spec gives one 40-mark source-based question assessing AO1, AO2 and AO4 (writing accuracy) with no AO3. On top of that, four quotations are fabricated or wrong (the Eel Marsh House 'bony old woman' simile, 'desperate, wild, grief', the funeral 'veil' and 'bones showed through', the closing line), three plot facts are wrong (Arthur indoors when he hears the trap, forcing the nursery door, Jennet's cause of death), and two characters are mislabelled (Keckwick for Samuel Daily, Jerome as a solicitor). 181 edits written.
